questions.enonce_markdown:
Define the following terms:

(i) Filter feeding.

(ii) Fluid feeding.

(iii) Detrital feeding. *[8 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Filter feeding (suspension feeding)** is a method of feeding in which an animal **strains small food particles (plankton, tiny organisms and organic particles) suspended in water** using a filtering structure, such as gills, cilia, setae or baleen plates. Examples: mussels and oysters (gills and cilia), *Daphnia* (setae on the legs), tadpoles, sponges, and baleen whales.

**(ii) Fluid feeding** is a method of feeding in which an animal **takes in food that is already in liquid form** (the body fluids or sap of another organism, or nectar), usually through mouthparts adapted for piercing and sucking or for sucking. Examples: mosquitoes and tsetse flies (blood), aphids (phloem sap, with a stylet), butterflies and bees (nectar), leeches (blood).

**(iii) Detrital feeding (detritivory)** is a method of feeding on **detritus**, that is, **dead and decaying organic matter** (fallen leaves, dead remains, faeces) found in the soil or at the bottom of water. The animals (detritivores) break it into smaller pieces, which speeds up decomposition by microorganisms. Examples: earthworms, woodlice, millipedes, termites, and many crabs and sea cucumbers.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Outline the role of the following cells in digestion:

(i) Parietal cells.

(ii) Chief cells.

(iii) Paneth cells.

(iv) Goblet cells. *[12 marks]* *(8, 12 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
| Cell | Where found | Role in digestion |
|---|---|---|
| **Parietal (oxyntic) cells** | Walls of the gastric glands in the stomach | Secrete **hydrochloric acid** (gastric pH about 1.5 to 2), which kills most bacteria in the food, gives the acid pH needed by pepsin, activates pepsinogen to pepsin and softens food. They also secrete **intrinsic factor**, needed to absorb vitamin B$_{12}$ in the ileum. |
| **Chief (peptic or zymogen) cells** | Deep in the gastric glands of the stomach | Secrete the **inactive enzyme pepsinogen**, activated by HCl to **pepsin**, which breaks proteins into shorter polypeptides. Being secreted inactive, it does not digest the cells that make it. In infants they also secrete rennin (chymosin), which clots milk protein. |
| **Paneth cells** | Base of the crypts of Lieberkuhn in the small intestine | Secrete **lysozyme** and antibacterial peptides (**defensins**), which kill bacteria and control the population of gut bacteria; they may also secrete some digestive enzymes and engulf bacteria. They protect the intestinal lining and so help digestion to continue safely. |
| **Goblet cells** | Lining of the stomach, small and large intestine, and the oesophagus | Secrete **mucus**, a slippery glycoprotein, which **lubricates** food for movement along the gut and **protects the lining** from digestive enzymes and from acid (in the stomach), and from mechanical damage. In the large intestine mucus binds the faeces. |

**Summary.** Parietal cells give the acid, chief cells give the protein-digesting enzyme precursor, goblet cells protect and lubricate, and Paneth cells guard the gut against microbes.
